\title{Submission A solution to Problem 8}
\date{}
\maketitle

\begin{center}
{\bf A polar transform for the relative Dressian}
\end{center}

\section*{0. Conventions and two local facts}

Let $E$ be the ground set, $r=\rk M$, and $\mu_M$ the trivial rank $r$
valuated matroid supported on the bases of $M$.  I use the standard
model of the relative Dressian: a rank $k$ point is a projective
valuated matroid $\nu$ with $\nu\preceq\mu_M$, where $\preceq$ denotes
valuated quotient.  Brandt--Eur--Zhang \cite{BEZ} identify this order with
inclusion of projective tropical linear spaces,
\[
        \Trop(\theta)\subseteq\Trop(\nu)
        \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \theta\preceq\nu .
\]
For valuated matroids $p,q$ of ranks $a\le b$, $p\preceq q$ is
equivalent to the incidence-Plucker relations
\[
 \min_{i\in J\setminus I}\{p(I\cup i)+q(J\setminus i)\}
 \quad\hbox{attained at least twice}                         \tag{IP}
\]
for all $I\in\binom{E}{a-1}$ and $J\in\binom{E}{b+1}$.  All-$\infty$
minima are regarded as attained at every displayed index.

\begin{criterion}[nested incidence suffices]\label{crit:local}
Let $p,q$ be valuated matroids of ranks $a<b$ whose ordinary supports
are in quotient order.  If {\rm (IP)} holds whenever $I\subseteq J$,
then {\rm (IP)} holds for all $I,J$.
\end{criterion}

\begin{proof}
For a rank $a$ valuated matroid $p$ and an $(a-1)$-set $I$, write
$C^*_p(I)_e=p(I\cup e)$, with value $\infty$ if $e\in I$.  We use the
standard cocircuit-generation theorem of Dress--Wenzel/Speyer \cite{DW,Speyer}: the
tropical linear space of a valuated matroid is the closed tropical convex
hull of its valuated cocircuits.

Fix arbitrary $I\in\binom{E}{a-1}$ and $J\in\binom{E}{b+1}$, and put
$c_j=q(J\setminus j)$ for $j\in J$.  If all $c_j$ are $\infty$ there is
nothing to prove.  Otherwise $J$ contains a $q$-basis.  Since the
ordinary support of $p$ is a quotient of the ordinary support of $q$,
every $q$-basis spans the support matroid of $p$ (indeed,
$a-\rk_p(Q)\le b-\rk_q(Q)=0$ for a $q$-basis $Q$); hence the
restriction $p|J$ has rank $a$.

For every $S\subseteq J$ with $|S|=a-1$, the nested hypothesis with
upper set $J$ says precisely that the cocircuit $C^*_{p|J}(S)$ is
tropically orthogonal to $c=(c_j)_{j\in J}$.  The set of vectors
orthogonal to a fixed $c$ is a tropical hyperplane, hence is tropically
convex; therefore it contains the whole tropical linear space of $p|J$.
It remains only to note that $C^*_p(I)|_J$ is a vector of $p|J$: for
each valuated circuit of $p|J$, indexed by a set
$D\in\binom{J}{a+1}$, the orthogonality relation
\[
 \min_{e\in D}\{p(I\cup e)+p(D\setminus e)\}
\]
is exactly a Plucker relation for $p$.  Hence $C^*_p(I)|_J$ is
orthogonal to $c$, which is the desired arbitrary incidence relation.
\end{proof}

We also use Wang's codimension-one theorem in the following precise
form.  In Wang's terminology the ``three-term incidence relations''
consist of degenerate, parallel, and concurrent hyperplane relations;
the displayed tropical minimum below is only the concurrent relation.

\begin{proposition}[elementary quotient test]\label{prop:elementarytest}
Let $\eta$ be a rank $d$ valuated matroid and let
$\theta:\binom{E}{d-1}\to{\mathbb R}\cup\{\infty\}$ be nonzero.  Suppose
that
\[
        \theta(A)=\infty\quad\hbox{whenever }A
        \hbox{ is dependent in the support matroid of }\eta              \tag{D}
\]
and, when $d\ge2$, for every $S\in\binom{E}{d-2}$ and distinct $x,y,z\notin S$,
\[
\min\{\theta(Sx)+\eta(Syz),\,
      \theta(Sy)+\eta(Sxz),\,
      \theta(Sz)+\eta(Sxy)\}                                      \tag{C}
\]
is attained at least twice.  Then $\theta$ is a valuated matroid and
$\theta\preceq\eta$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For $d=1$ this is the unique rank-zero quotient.  Let $d\ge2$.  By
Wang's Theorem 4.3 \cite{Wang}, $\Dr^1(\eta)$ is cut out by the
degenerate, parallel, and concurrent three-term incidence relations.
Condition (D) is exactly the degenerate part, and (C) contains the
concurrent part.  It remains only to see that the parallel part follows
from (C).  Write $A=Di$ and $B=Dj$ for independent $(d-1)$-sets in the
support matroid of $\eta$ with the same closure, and choose $k$ outside
that closure, so $Dik$ and $Djk$ are bases.  Applying (C) to
$D,i,j,k$, the third upper coordinate $\eta(Dij)$ is $\infty$, while
$\eta(Dik)$ and $\eta(Djk)$ are finite.  Hence
\[
        \theta(Di)+\eta(Djk)=\theta(Dj)+\eta(Dik),
\]
which is Wang's parallel hyperplane relation.  Thus all of Wang's
defining relations hold, so $\theta$ represents a codimension-one
tropical linear subspace of $\Trop(\eta)$.
\end{proof}

Finally, if $\nu\preceq\mu_M$ has rank $k$, we use its valuated Higgs
completion
\[
 h_j(B)=
 \begin{cases}
 \min\{\nu(C): B\subseteq C,\ |C|=k\}, & j\le k,\ |B|=j,\\
 \min\{\nu(C): C\subseteq B,\ |C|=k\}, & j\ge k,\ B\in\mathcal I_j(M),\\
 \infty, & j\ge k,\ B\notin\mathcal I_j(M).
 \end{cases}                                                \tag{1}
\]
Murota's truncation and relative elongation theorems \cite[Theorems 2.1 and 4.1]{Murota}, equivalently the
Dress--Terhalle well-layering construction \cite{DT}, give valuated matroids
$h_j$ and adjacent quotients $h_j\preceq h_{j+1}$.  The top layer is
projectively $\mu_M$: if $B'=B-e+f$ are adjacent $M$-bases and
$C\subseteq B$ minimizes (1), then either $e\notin C$ and $C\subseteq B'$,
or the incidence relation for $\nu\preceq\mu_M$ with lower set $C-e$ and
upper set $B\cup f$ gives a $k$-subset of $B'$ of value at most
$\nu(C)$; by symmetry the two top-layer values are equal.

\section*{1. Flat-lattice duality and flat constancy}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:modular}
If $\cL(M)$ admits an order-reversing involution $X\mapsto X^\perp$,
then $\cL(M)$ is modular and $\rk(X^\perp)=r-\rk(X)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The anti-automorphism reverses maximal chains, so it sends rank $i$ to
rank $r-i$.  Applying it to the semimodular inequality for the geometric
lattice $\cL(M)$ gives the reverse inequality, hence equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[flat constancy]\label{lem:flatconst}
Let $\nu\preceq\mu_M$ have rank $k$.  If $B,B'$ are independent
$k$-subsets of $M$ with $\cl(B)=\cl(B')$, then $\nu(B)=\nu(B')$; and
$\nu(A)=\infty$ whenever $A$ is dependent in $M$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The support matroid of $\nu$ is an ordinary quotient of $M$, so its
bases are independent in $M$.  For $k>0$ it suffices to compare
$B=A\cup b$ and $B'=A\cup b'$ spanning the same rank $k$ flat.  Choose
one complement $C$ so that both $AbC$ and $Ab'C$ are $M$-bases.  In the
incidence relation for $\nu\preceq\mu_M$ with lower set $A$ and upper
set $A\cup\{b,b'\}\cup C$, the only finite $\mu_M$-terms are the
$b$- and $b'$-terms.  Thus $\nu(Ab)=\nu(Ab')$.
\end{proof}

Write $\bar\nu(X)$ for the common value on independent $k$-sets spanning
the rank $k$ flat $X$, and put $\bar\nu(X)=\infty$ if no basis of $\nu$
spans $X$.

\section*{2. The polar transform}

For a rank $k$ quotient $\nu\preceq\mu_M$ define
\[
 \nu^{\perp_M}(A)=
 \begin{cases}
   \bar\nu\bigl((\cl A)^\perp\bigr),
      & A\text{ independent in }M,\ |A|=r-k,\\
   \infty,&\text{otherwise.}
 \end{cases}                                                 \tag{2}
\]
This is projectively well-defined, and applying it twice recovers the
original flat coordinates.

\begin{lemma}[ordinary polar rank]\label{lem:ordinary}
Let $N$ be an ordinary quotient of $M$ of rank $k$, with rank function
$\rho_N$.  Then
\[
        \rho^\perp(A)=\rk_M(A)-k+\rho_N((\cl A)^\perp)          \tag{3}
\]
is a matroid rank function.  Its bases are precisely the finite support
of (2).  If $N_p$ is a quotient of $N_q$, then
$N_q^{\perp_M}$ is a quotient of $N_p^{\perp_M}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since $N$ is a quotient of $M$, $\rho_N$ is constant on $M$-closures:
if $e\in\cl_M(A)$, then the $N$-rank increment from $A$ to $Ae$ is at
most the corresponding $M$-increment, namely $0$.  First restrict (3) to
flats.  For flats $X\le Y$,
\[
\rho^\perp(Y)-\rho^\perp(X)
 =\rk(Y)-\rk(X)-\bigl(\rho_N(X^\perp)-\rho_N(Y^\perp)\bigr)
\]
is between $0$ and $\rk(Y)-\rk(X)$ by the strong-map increment
inequality, so $\rho^\perp$ is monotone with unit increments on flats.
For flats $X,Y$, modularity of $\rk_M$ and the identities
$(X\wedge Y)^\perp=X^\perp\vee Y^\perp$ and
$(X\vee Y)^\perp=X^\perp\wedge Y^\perp$ reduce submodularity of
$\rho^\perp$ to submodularity of $\rho_N$.

For arbitrary subsets, $\rho^\perp(A)=\rho^\perp(\cl_M A)$.  If
$X=\cl A$ and $Y=\cl B$, then
$\cl(A\cap B)\le X\wedge Y$ and $\cl(A\cup B)=X\vee Y$; by monotonicity
on flats, submodularity for $X,Y$ implies submodularity for $A,B$.
The unit-increment property also passes from flats to subsets.  Thus
(3) is a matroid rank function.  An $M$-independent set $A$ of size
$r-k$ has full $\rho^\perp$-rank exactly when
$\rho_N((\cl A)^\perp)=k$, and $M$-dependent sets cannot be bases; this
is precisely the finite support of (2).

If $N_p$ is a quotient of $N_q$, then on every interval the rank
increment of $N_p$ is at most that of $N_q$.  The displayed formula for
increments therefore reverses the inequality for the polar ranks, which
is exactly the strong-map criterion saying that $N_q^{\perp_M}$ is a
quotient of $N_p^{\perp_M}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[elementary opposition]\label{lem:elementary}
Let $p\preceq q\preceq\mu_M$, with $\rk p=d$ and $\rk q=d+1$.  Then
$q^{\perp_M}$ and $p^{\perp_M}$ satisfy all adjacent three-term
relations of ranks $r-d-1$ and $r-d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix $A$ of size $r-d-2$ and distinct $x,y,z\notin A$.  Put
$U=\cl(A)$, $W=\cl(Axyz)$, and $\delta=\rk W-\rk U$.  If $A$ is
dependent, or if $\delta\le1$, each term contains a dependent set of the
required size and hence is $\infty$.

If $\delta=2$, let $G=W^\perp$ and $H=U^\perp$, of ranks $d$ and
$d+2$.  Whenever the term indexed by $x$ is finite, $Ayz$ spans $W$,
so its $p$-factor is the common value $\bar p(G)$; its $q$-factor is
$\bar q((\cl(Ax))^\perp)$, and similarly for $y,z$.  In the rank-two
interval $[U,W]$, a loop over $U$ makes all terms involving it
infinite, and two parallel elements give equal corresponding
$q$-coordinates.  Thus only the case of three non-parallel points over
$U$ needs proof.  Choose a basis $S$ of $G$, representatives
$a_x,a_y,a_z$ for the three dual rank-one flats over $G$ in $[G,H]$,
and a complement $C$ of $H$ to a basis of $M$.  In the incidence
relation for $q\preceq\mu_M$ with lower set $S$ and upper set
$S\cup\{a_x,a_y,a_z\}\cup C$, the only finite $\mu_M$-terms are those
obtained by deleting one of $a_x,a_y,a_z$.  Hence the three displayed
$q$-coordinates have a non-unique minimum; adding the common
$\bar p(G)$ proves the transformed relation.

If $\delta=3$, then $x,y,z$ form a Boolean frame over $U$.  Let
$G=W^\perp$ and
\[
 P_x=(\cl(Ayz))^\perp,\quad P_y=(\cl(Axz))^\perp,\quad
 P_z=(\cl(Axy))^\perp .
\]
These are the three atoms over $G$ in the dual frame, and
$(\cl(Ax))^\perp=P_y\vee P_z$, with the analogous identities for
$y,z$.  Choose a basis $S$ of $G$ and representatives
$a_e\in P_e\setminus G$.  The adjacent incidence relation for
$p\preceq q$ applied to the lower set $S$ and to
$S\cup\{a_x,a_y,a_z\}$ is exactly the transformed three-term relation,
using flat constancy to identify the displayed coordinates.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:set}
The formula $\nu\mapsto\nu^{\perp_M}$ defines an involution of the set
underlying $\Dr(M)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Insert $\nu$ in the complete flag (1).  We prove inductively that
\[
        h_r^{\perp_M}\preceq h_{r-1}^{\perp_M}\preceq\cdots
        \preceq h_0^{\perp_M}=\mu_M .
\]
After harmless scalar normalization, the right endpoint
$h_0^{\perp_M}=\mu_M$ is clear from (2).  If $r\le1$, there is
nothing more to check beyond the automatic rank-zero quotient.  Now assume $r\ge2$.
Suppose $0\le j\le r-2$ and $h_j^{\perp_M}$ has
already been proved valuated.  Since $h_j\preceq h_{j+1}$, Lemma
\ref{lem:ordinary} says that the ordinary support of
$h_{j+1}^{\perp_M}$ is an elementary quotient of the ordinary support of
$h_j^{\perp_M}$; in particular it satisfies the degenerate support
condition (D) relative to $h_j^{\perp_M}$.  Lemma
\ref{lem:elementary} gives the displayed concurrent relations (C) for
the pair $h_{j+1}^{\perp_M},h_j^{\perp_M}$.  Proposition
\ref{prop:elementarytest} then implies
$h_{j+1}^{\perp_M}\preceq h_j^{\perp_M}$.  This proves the induction
down to $h_{r-1}^{\perp_M}$; the last rank-zero quotient
$h_r^{\perp_M}\preceq h_{r-1}^{\perp_M}$ is automatic.  Hence $\nu^{\perp_M}$, one layer of the flag, lies in
$\Dr(M)$.  Involutivity follows from (2) and $(X^\perp)^\perp=X$.
\end{proof}

\section*{3. Order reversal}

\begin{lemma}[circuit minima]\label{lem:circuit}
Let $w\preceq\mu_M$ have rank $k\ge1$, let $A$ be an independent
$(k-1)$-set of $M$, and let $C$ be a circuit of $M/A$ with $|C|\ge2$.
Then $\min_{i\in C}w(A\cup i)$ is attained at least twice.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $F=\cl(A\cup C)$.  For every $i\in C$, $A\cup(C-i)$ is independent
and spans $F$.  Choose one complement $D$ of $F$ to an $M$-basis.  In
the incidence relation for $w\preceq\mu_M$ with lower set $A$ and upper
set $A\cup C\cup D$, the finite $\mu_M$-terms are exactly those indexed
by $i\in C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:order}
If $p\preceq q\preceq\mu_M$, then
\[
        q^{\perp_M}\preceq p^{\perp_M}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $\rk p=a$ and $\rk q=b$.  If $a=b$, the strong-map inequalities applied to
$\emptyset\subseteq A$ and to $A\subseteq E$ force the two ordinary
support rank functions to be equal.  Then $p$ and $q$ are projectively
equal: the equal-rank incidence relation on adjacent bases shows
$p(B)-q(B)$ is constant on the common basis graph.  If $a=0$, then $p^{\perp_M}=\mu_M$, so the
assertion is $q^{\perp_M}\preceq\mu_M$; if $b=r$, it is the vacuous
rank-zero lower quotient.  Hence assume $0<a<b<r$.

By Proposition \ref{prop:set} the polars are valuated matroids, and by
Lemma \ref{lem:ordinary} their ordinary supports are in quotient order.
By Criterion \ref{crit:local} it remains to prove nested incidence.
Fix $A\subseteq T$ with
$|A|=r-b-1$, $|T|=r-a+1$, set $B=T\setminus A$, and
$m=|B|=b-a+2$.  If $A$ is dependent all terms are $\infty$.  Otherwise
put $U=\cl(A)$, $W=\cl(T)$, and $\delta=\rk W-\rk U$.  A finite term
forces $T-i$ to be independent, hence $\delta\ge m-1$; since
$\delta\le m$, only two cases remain.

If $\delta=m$, then $T$ is independent over $U$.  Let $G=W^\perp$ and
$H=U^\perp$, of ranks $a-1$ and $b+1$.  The interval generated by $B$
is Boolean; after applying $^\perp$, the flats
$X_i=(\cl(T-i))^\perp$ are the atoms over $G$, and
$Y_i=(\cl(Ai))^\perp$ is the join of all $X_j$ with $j\ne i$.  Choose a
basis $S$ of $G$ and representatives $x_i\in X_i\setminus G$.  The
nested incidence relation for $p\preceq q$ with lower set $S$ and upper
set $S\cup\{x_i:i\in B\}$ is exactly the desired transformed relation.

If $\delta=m-1$, then $B$ has nullity one in $M/A$, hence a unique
circuit $C$.  A loop circuit gives only $\infty$ terms.  Otherwise, for
$i\notin C$ the set $T-i$ is dependent; for $i\in C$ it is independent
and spans $W$, so the $p^{\perp_M}(T-i)$ factor is the common value
$\bar p(W^\perp)$.  Lemma \ref{lem:circuit}, applied to
$w=q^{\perp_M}$ and the circuit $C$ of $M/A$, gives two minima among
the remaining $q^{\perp_M}(Ai)$ terms.  This proves nested incidence.
\end{proof}

\section*{4. Agreement with flats}

Let $F$ be a flat of rank $f$, and let $q_F$ be the trivial rank
$r-f$ valuated matroid of $M/F\oplus U_{0,F}$.  For an independent
$(r-f)$-set $B$ with $Z=\cl(B)$,
\[
        q_F(B)<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Z\vee F=\hat1.
\]
For an independent $f$-set $A$ with $Y=\cl(A)$, formula (2) gives
\[
 q_F^{\perp_M}(A)<\infty
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Y^\perp\vee F=\hat1 .
\]
By modularity, since $\rk(Y^\perp)=r-f$ and $\rk F=f$, this is
equivalent to $Y^\perp\wedge F=\hat0$.  Applying the anti-automorphism
gives $Y\vee F^\perp=\hat1$, the basis condition for
$M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}$.  The finite values are zero on both
sides.  Thus the polar transform sends the flat $F$ to $F^\perp$.

Combining Proposition \ref{prop:set}, Theorem \ref{thm:order}, and this
flat computation, the map
\[
        \Phi([\nu])=[\nu^{\perp_M}]
\]
is an order-reversing involution of $\Dr(M)$ extending the given
order-reversing involution of $\cL(M)$.

\title{Submission B solution to Problem 8}
\date{}
\maketitle

\section*{Overview and scope}

The original question asks whether an order-reversing involution on the flat lattice of a matroid extends to an order-reversing involution of the relative Dressian.  The theorem proved here is the finite-ground-set version.  The proof first reduces to the simplification of the matroid.  In the simple case, the existence of a flat-lattice anti-involution forces the lattice of flats to be modular.  Modularity then implies that every valuated quotient is constant on the bases of each flat, which permits the construction of a dual, or ``dagger,'' valuated quotient.

The main work is to prove that the dagger construction is again a valuated quotient, that it is involutive, and that it depends only on the tropical linear space rather than on the chosen valuated Pluecker vector.  The first point is proved by checking the support matroid, the tropical Pluecker relations, and the quotient circuit criterion.  The second is formal from the definition.  The third is an annihilator statement using polar bases.  Finally the construction is transported back from the simplification to the original finite matroid.

\begin{theorem}[Established finite-ground-set theorem]\label{thm:main}
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on ground set \(E\).  Suppose that the lattice of flats \(\cL(M)\) admits an order-reversing involution
\[
F\longmapsto F^\perp .
\]
Let \(\Dr(M)\) be the poset, ordered by inclusion, of projective tropical linear spaces contained in \(\Trop(M)\).  Then there is an order-reversing involution
\[
\Phi:\Dr(M)\longrightarrow \Dr(M)
\]
such that, for every flat \(F\in \cL(M)\),
\[
\Phi\!\left(\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})\right)
=
\Trop(M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}),
\]
where \(U_{0,F}\) denotes the rank-zero matroid on \(F\), and the direct sums are considered as matroids on \(E\).
\end{theorem}

\section*{Preliminaries}

We use the min-plus semiring \(\T=\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}\).  Tropical projective space is obtained from \(\T^E\setminus\{(\infty,\ldots,\infty)\}\) by quotienting by simultaneous tropical scalar translation; in affine-cone calculations we allow the all-\(\infty\) vector.

A rank \(k\) valuated matroid on \(E\) is a function
\[
p:\binom{E}{k}\to \T
\]
not identically \(\infty\), satisfying the tropical Pluecker relations; we extend \(p\) to all subsets by \(p_I=\infty\) when \(|I|\ne k\).  Its tropical linear space is
\[
\Trop(p)=
\left\{
x\in \TP^{E-1}:
\text{ for all }J\in\binomE{k+1},\ 
\min_{j\in J}(x_j+p_{J-j})\text{ has no unique finite minimizer}
\right\}.
\]
An ordinary matroid \(M\) of rank \(r\) is identified with the constant valuated matroid \(p^M\), where \(p^M_B=0\) for bases \(B\) of \(M\), and \(p^M_B=\infty\) otherwise.  A valuated matroid \(p\) is called a valuated quotient of \(M\) if \(\Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(M)\).  Thus \(\Dr(M)\) is the set of all projective spaces \(\Trop(p)\), with \(p\) a valuated quotient of \(M\), ordered by inclusion.

We use standard facts from valuated matroid theory: the support of a valuated matroid is an ordinary matroid; support plus the three-term tropical Pluecker relations characterize valuated matroids; tropical linear spaces are the tropical convex hulls of their valuated cocircuits; and tropical hyperplanes are tropically convex.  These are due to Dress--Wenzel and Murota--Tamura and are used in the standard treatments by Speyer and by Maclagan--Sturmfels; see also Hampe for tropical convexity \cite{DW92,MT01,Speyer08,MS15,Hampe15}.  For flats of \(M\), we write
\[
G\wedge H=G\cap H,\qquad G\vee H=\cl_M(G\cup H).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Quotient criterion and support consequences]\label{lem:quotient}
Let \(p\) be a rank \(k\) valuated matroid on \(E\), and for \(A\in\binomE{k-1}\) put \(C_A(e)=p_{A\cup e}\).
\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(k>0\), then \(\Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(M)\) if and only if, for every circuit \(C\) of \(M\) and every \(A\in\binomE{k-1}\),
\[
\min_{c\in C\setminus A}p_{A\cup c}
\]
has no unique finite minimizer.  If \(k=0\), then \(\Trop(p)\) is empty projectively and \(p\) is automatically a quotient.
\item If \(p\) is a quotient and \(N=\supp(p)\), then:
\[
I\text{ dependent in }M,\ |I|=k \Longrightarrow p_I=\infty;
\]
\[
\rk_N(A)=\rk_N(\cl_M(A))\quad\text{for all }A\subseteq E;
\]
and for flats \(G\subseteq H\) of \(M\),
\[
\rk_N(H)-\rk_N(G)\le \rk_M(H)-\rk_M(G).
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The Bergman fan \(\Trop(M)\) is cut out by the circuit hyperplanes
\[
\min_{c\in C}x_c\quad\text{has no unique finite minimizer}
\]
for circuits \(C\) of \(M\).  Also \(\Trop(p)\) is the tropical convex hull of the valuated cocircuits \(C_A\), and tropical hyperplanes are tropically convex.  Hence \(\Trop(p)\subseteq\Trop(M)\) exactly when every \(C_A\) satisfies every circuit equation of \(M\), which is the displayed criterion.  For \(k=0\), the rank-zero tropical linear space has only the all-\(\infty\) affine vector, hence no projective point.

Now assume \(p\) is a quotient.  If \(I\in\binomE{k}\) is \(M\)-dependent, choose an \(M\)-circuit \(C\subseteq I\) and \(c\in C\).  With \(A=I-c\), the criterion gives a one-term minimum \(p_I\); therefore \(p_I=\infty\).

We next prove \(\rk_N(A)=\rk_N(\cl_M(A))\).  It is enough to show \(\cl_M(A)\subseteq\cl_N(A)\).  Let \(C\) be an \(M\)-circuit.  If some \(e\in C\) were a coloop of \(N|C\), then there would be an \(N\)-hyperplane \(H\) containing \(C-e\) but not \(e\).  Choose an \(N\)-basis \(A\) of \(H\).  Then \(A\cup e\) is an \(N\)-basis while \(A\cup c\) is \(N\)-dependent for every \(c\in C-e\), contradicting the quotient criterion.  Thus no element of \(C\) is a coloop of \(N|C\), so every element of \(C\) lies in an \(N\)-circuit contained in \(C\).  If \(e\in\cl_M(A)\), choose an \(M\)-circuit \(C\subseteq A\cup e\) containing \(e\); an \(N\)-circuit in \(C\) containing \(e\) proves \(e\in\cl_N(A)\).

Finally, if \(G\subseteq H\) are \(M\)-flats, choose \(S\subseteq H\) with \(\cl_M(G\cup S)=H\) and \(|S|=\rk_M(H)-\rk_M(G)\).  Then
\[
\rk_N(H)=\rk_N(G\cup S)\le \rk_N(G)+|S|,
\]
which is the desired inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Reduction to the simplification]\label{lem:simplification}
Let \(L_0=\cl_M(\varnothing)\) be the loop set of \(M\), let \(S=\operatorname{si}(M)\), let \(\bar E\) be the set of nonloop parallel classes, and let
\[
\pi:E\setminus L_0\to \bar E
\]
be the quotient map.  Define
\[
(\Delta x)_e=
\begin{cases}
\infty,& e\in L_0,\\
x_{\pi(e)},& e\notin L_0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\Delta\) induces a poset isomorphism \(\Dr(S)\cong \Dr(M)\).  Moreover, if \(F\in\cL(M)\) corresponds to \(\bar F\in\cL(S)\), then
\[
\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})
=
\Delta\bigl(\Trop(S/\bar F\oplus U_{0,\bar F})\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Every flat of \(M\) contains \(L_0\) and is a union of nonloop parallel classes, so \(\cL(M)\cong\cL(S)\).

Let \(p\) be a rank \(k\) quotient of \(M\).  By Lemma \ref{lem:quotient}, every \(M\)-dependent \(k\)-set has value \(\infty\).  Hence no finite basis contains a loop or two parallel elements.  If \(e,f\) are parallel nonloops and \(A\cap\{e,f\}=\varnothing\), the circuit \(\{e,f\}\) gives \(p_{A\cup e}=p_{A\cup f}\).  Therefore \(p\) descends uniquely to a valuated matroid \(\bar p\) on \(\bar E\).  The tropical Pluecker relations and the quotient circuit criterion for \(\bar p\) are obtained from those for \(p\), because circuits of \(S\) are precisely images of nonloop circuits of \(M\) after deleting parallel repetitions.  Thus \(\bar p\) is a quotient of \(S\).

Conversely, if \(q\) is a quotient of \(S\), define
\[
q^\uparrow_I=
\begin{cases}
q_{\pi(I)},& I\cap L_0=\varnothing\text{ and }\pi\text{ is injective on }I,\\
\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The Pluecker relations for \(q^\uparrow\) either reduce under \(\pi\) to those for \(q\), or are trivial because all finite terms occur in equal parallel pairs.  The quotient criterion for \(M\) follows from the quotient criterion for \(S\), together with the loop circuits and two-element parallel circuits.  Thus \(q^\uparrow\) is a quotient of \(M\).

The tropical equations of \(q^\uparrow\) force loop coordinates to be \(\infty\) and force equality along each nonloop parallel class; after this identification the remaining equations are exactly those of \(q\).  Hence \(\Trop(q^\uparrow)=\Delta(\Trop(q))\), and inclusions are preserved and reflected.  This proves the poset isomorphism.  The final displayed identity is the same statement applied to the ordinary quotient \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\), whose simplification is \(S/\bar F\oplus U_{0,\bar F}\).
\end{proof}

\section*{The simple case}

Assume in this section that \(M\) is simple of rank \(r\), and that \(\cL(M)\) has the given order-reversing involution.

\begin{lemma}[Modularity and flat constancy]\label{lem:modflat}
The matroid \(M\) is modular:
\[
\rk_M(G)+\rk_M(H)=\rk_M(G\wedge H)+\rk_M(G\vee H)
\]
for all flats \(G,H\).  Also \(\rk_M(F^\perp)=r-\rk_M(F)\).  If \(p\) is a rank \(k\) valuated quotient of \(M\), then \(p_I=p_{I'}\) whenever \(I,I'\) are \(M\)-bases of the same rank \(k\) flat.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(M\) is simple, \(\cL(M)\) is a finite geometric lattice, hence semimodular.  The anti-involution sends maximal chains from \(\varnothing\) to \(F\) to maximal chains from \(F^\perp\) to \(E\), so \(\rk(F^\perp)=r-\rk(F)\).  Applying semimodularity to \(G,H\) gives ``\(\ge\)'' in the modular identity.  Applying semimodularity to \(G^\perp,H^\perp\) and using rank reversal gives the opposite inequality, hence equality.

For flat constancy, the basis graph of \(M|F\) is connected, so it suffices to compare \(I=A\cup a\) and \(I'=A\cup b\).  Since \(\cl(Aa)=\cl(Ab)=F\), there is an \(M\)-circuit \(C\subseteq A\cup\{a,b\}\) containing both \(a\) and \(b\).  Lemma \ref{lem:quotient} applied to \(C\) and \(A\) says the minimum of \(p_{Aa}\) and \(p_{Ab}\) has no unique finite minimizer; therefore \(p_{Aa}=p_{Ab}\), allowing both sides to be \(\infty\).
\end{proof}

For a rank \(k\) quotient \(p\), write
\[
\bar p(F)=p_I
\]
when \(F\) is a rank \(k\) flat and \(I\) is any \(M\)-basis of \(F\).  This is well-defined by Lemma \ref{lem:modflat}.  Put \(n=r-k\), and define
\[
p^\dagger_J=
\begin{cases}
\bar p(\cl_M(J)^\perp),& |J|=n\text{ and }J\text{ is }M\text{-independent},\\
\infty,& |J|=n\text{ and }J\text{ is }M\text{-dependent}.
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{lemma}[Local dual Pluecker relation]\label{lem:local}
Let \(p\) be a rank \(k\) quotient of \(M\).  Let \(Y\) be a rank \(k+2\) flat and let \(H_1,H_2,H_3,H_4\) be hyperplanes of \(Y\).  Define
\[
[ij]=
\begin{cases}
\bar p(H_i\wedge H_j),&H_i\ne H_j,\\
\infty,&H_i=H_j.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
\min\bigl([12]+[34],\ [13]+[24],\ [14]+[23]\bigr)
\]
has no unique finite minimizer.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If two hyperplanes are equal, say \(H_1=H_2\), then \([12]=\infty\), while \([13]=[23]\) and \([14]=[24]\); hence the last two sums are equal.  Assume now that the \(H_i\) are distinct, and put \(Z=H_1\wedge H_2\wedge H_3\wedge H_4\).  In the modular interval \([\varnothing,Y]\), \(\rk(Z)\in\{k-2,k-1,k\}\).

If \(\rk(Z)=k\), every pairwise meet is \(Z\), so all three sums are equal.  If \(\rk(Z)=k-2\), work in the rank-four interval \([Z,Y]\).  Let \(T_i=\bigwedge_{j\ne i}H_j\).  Modularity gives \(\rk(T_i/Z)=1\): it is at least \(1\), and if it were at least \(2\), then \(T_i\wedge H_i\) would have positive relative rank, contradicting \(T_i\wedge H_i=Z\).  For \(\{i,j,m,n\}=\{1,2,3,4\}\), one has \(H_i\wedge H_j=T_m\vee T_n\).  Choose a basis \(A\) of \(Z\) and \(t_i\in T_i\setminus Z\).  Then, for example, \([12]=p_{A t_3t_4}\) and \([34]=p_{A t_1t_2}\), and the desired relation is the three-term tropical Pluecker relation for \(p\) on \(A,t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4\).

It remains to treat \(\rk(Z)=k-1\).  In the rank-three modular geometry \([Z,Y]\), define \(w(P)=\bar p(P)\) for points \(P\).  We first show \(w\in\Trop([Z,Y])\).  Let \(D\) be a circuit of this geometry, choose a basis \(A\) of \(Z\), and choose \(e_P\in P\setminus Z\) for \(P\in D\).  A circuit of the contraction by \(Z\) lifts to an \(M\)-circuit \(C\subseteq Z\cup\{e_P:P\in D\}\) whose image is \(D\).  Applying Lemma \ref{lem:quotient} to \(C\) and \(A\), the elements in \(Z\) contribute \(\infty\), and the remaining values are \(w(P)\).  Thus \(w\in\Trop([Z,Y])\).

We use the following elementary rank-three fact.  If \(G\) is a finite simple modular rank-three matroid, \(w\in\Trop(G)\), and \(L_1,\ldots,L_4\) are distinct lines, then
\[
\min_{\text{matchings}}
\bigl(w(L_i\wedge L_j)+w(L_m\wedge L_n)\bigr)
\]
has no unique finite minimizer.  Indeed, for the min convention, \(w\in\Trop(G)\) iff every superlevel set \(\{x:w_x\ge\lambda\}\) is a flat: a nonclosed superlevel set gives a circuit with a unique minimum outside it, and conversely a unique circuit minimum gives such a superlevel set.  In rank three the nontrivial superlevel flats form a chain \(a\le B\), where \(a\) is a point and \(B\) a line; after subtracting the minimum,
\[
w(x)=\lambda{\bf 1}_{x=a}+\mu{\bf 1}_{x\le B},\qquad \lambda,\mu\in[0,\infty].
\]
If none of the \(L_i\) equals \(B\), color \(L_i\) by \(y_i=L_i\wedge B\).  A pair \(L_i,L_j\) meets on \(B\) exactly when \(y_i=y_j\); otherwise its contribution is \(0\).  For four colored objects, by the multiplicities \(1+1+1+1,2+1+1,2+2,3+1,4\), the minimum over the three perfect matchings is never unique.  If, say, \(L_1=B\), put \(y_i=L_i\wedge B\) for \(i=2,3,4\) and \(c(y)=\lambda+\mu\) for \(y=a\), \(c(y)=\mu\) otherwise.  The three costs are
\[
c(y_2)+{\bf 1}_{y_3=y_4}c(y_3),\quad
c(y_3)+{\bf 1}_{y_2=y_4}c(y_2),\quad
c(y_4)+{\bf 1}_{y_2=y_3}c(y_2),
\]
and the cases ``all distinct'', ``exactly two equal'', and ``all equal'' give, respectively, at least two minimal costs, the two costs pairing \(B\) with one of the equal colors, or three equal costs.

Apply this fact to the lines \(H_i/Z\) in \([Z,Y]\).  Their pairwise meets are the flats \(H_i\wedge H_j\), so the desired relation follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The dagger construction is a valuated quotient]\label{lem:daggerquotient}
For every rank \(k\) valuated quotient \(p\) of the simple modular matroid \(M\), the function \(p^\dagger\) is a rank \(r-k\) valuated quotient of \(M\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The cases \(k=0\) and \(k=r\) are immediate: \(p^\dagger\) is respectively the constant valuated matroid of \(M\), or the unique rank-zero valuated matroid, up to adding a scalar.  Assume \(0<k<r\), put \(n=r-k\), and let \(N=\supp(p)\).

First determine the support.  For a flat \(G\), set
\[
\rho^\dagger(G)=\rk_M(G)-k+\rk_N(G^\perp),
\]
and extend by \(\rho^\dagger(A)=\rho^\dagger(\cl_M(A))\).  We have \(\rho^\dagger(\varnothing)=0\) and \(\rho^\dagger(E)=n\).  If \(G\subseteq H\) are flats, then \(H^\perp\subseteq G^\perp\), and Lemma \ref{lem:quotient} gives
\[
\rk_N(G^\perp)-\rk_N(H^\perp)\le \rk_M(G^\perp)-\rk_M(H^\perp)=\rk_M(H)-\rk_M(G),
\]
so \(\rho^\dagger\) is monotone.  For flats \(G,H\), modularity of \(M\), submodularity of \(\rk_N\), and the quotient property
\(\rk_N(A)=\rk_N(\cl_M A)\) give
\[
\rho^\dagger(G)+\rho^\dagger(H)\ge
\rho^\dagger(G\wedge H)+\rho^\dagger(G\vee H).
\]
For arbitrary \(A,B\), apply this to \(G=\cl_M(A)\), \(H=\cl_M(B)\), using \(\cl(A\cup B)=G\vee H\) and \(\cl(A\cap B)\subseteq G\wedge H\).  Thus \(\rho^\dagger\) is submodular.  Since
\[
0\le \rho^\dagger(A)\le \rk_M(A)\le |A|,
\]
and submodularity gives \(\rho^\dagger(A\cup e)-\rho^\dagger(A)\le\rho^\dagger(\{e\})\le 1\), this is a matroid rank function of rank \(n\).  Call the matroid \(N^\dagger\).

For \(J\in\binomE n\), the condition \(\rho^\dagger(J)=n\) forces \(J\) to be \(M\)-independent.  For such \(J\),
\[
\rho^\dagger(J)=n-k+\rk_N(\cl_M(J)^\perp),
\]
so \(J\) is a basis of \(N^\dagger\) iff \(\rk_N(\cl_M(J)^\perp)=k\), equivalently iff \(p^\dagger_J<\infty\).  Hence the finite support of \(p^\dagger\) is a matroid.

It remains to check the three-term tropical Pluecker relations.  Let \(S\in\binomE{n-2}\) and let \(a,b,c,d\notin S\) be distinct.  If \(S\) is dependent, or if some of \(a,b,c,d\) lies in \(X=\cl_M(S)\), all three Pluecker sums are \(\infty\).  Otherwise \(X\) has rank \(n-2\), \(Y=X^\perp\) has rank \(k+2\), and
\[
H_e=(X\vee e)^\perp\qquad(e=a,b,c,d)
\]
is a hyperplane of \(Y\).  If \(H_e=H_f\), then \(Sef\) is dependent and \(p^\dagger_{Sef}=\infty\); if \(H_e\ne H_f\), then \(Sef\) is independent and
\[
p^\dagger_{Sef}=\bar p(H_e\wedge H_f).
\]
Lemma \ref{lem:local} gives the required Pluecker relation.  Thus \(p^\dagger\) is a valuated matroid.

Finally we prove that it is a quotient of \(M\).  By Lemma \ref{lem:quotient}, let \(C\) be an \(M\)-circuit and \(A\in\binomE{n-1}\).  If \(A\) is dependent, all terms \(p^\dagger_{A\cup c}\) are \(\infty\).  Assume \(A\) is independent, put \(X=\cl_M(A)\), and \(Y=X^\perp\).  For a point \(P\) of the simplification of \(M/X\), equivalently a rank \(n\) flat \(P\) with \(X<P\), define
\[
u(P)=\bar p(P^\perp).
\]
We claim \(u\in\Trop(M/X)\).  By the superlevel-flat criterion, it suffices to show that every set \(\{P:u(P)\ge\lambda\}\) is a flat.  In a finite simple modular matroid, a line-closed point set is a flat: choose an independent spanning set \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) in it; by induction all points of \(H=\cl(a_1,\ldots,a_{m-1})\) are in it, and for \(x\in\cl(H,a_m)\setminus H\), modularity makes the line \(\cl(a_m,x)\) meet \(H\) in a point, so line-closure contains \(x\).

Thus it is enough to prove line-closure.  Let \(P_1,P_2\) be in the superlevel set and \(P_3\le P_1\vee P_2\) a point.  Put \(H_i=P_i^\perp\subseteq Y\).  Then \(H_3\supseteq H_1\wedge H_2\).  If \(H_3=H_1\) or \(H_2\), there is nothing to prove.  Otherwise \(H_1,H_2,H_3\) are distinct hyperplanes of \(Y\) containing \(Z=H_1\wedge H_2\), where \(\rk(Z)=k-1\).  Choose a basis \(B\) of \(Z\) and \(e_i\in H_i\setminus Z\).  In the rank-two interval \([Z,Y]\), the three points \(H_1,H_2,H_3\) form a circuit; lifting it to \(M\) and applying Lemma \ref{lem:quotient} to \(p\) and \(B\) shows that \(\min(u(P_1),u(P_2),u(P_3))\) has no unique finite minimizer.  Since \(u(P_1),u(P_2)\ge\lambda\), we get \(u(P_3)\ge\lambda\).  Hence \(u\in\Trop(M/X)\).

Return to \(C\).  If \(C\subseteq X\), all terms are \(\infty\).  Otherwise set \(D=C\setminus X\).  For \(c\in D\),
\[
p^\dagger_{A\cup c}=u(\cl_M(X\cup c)).
\]
Every element of \(D\) is contained in a circuit of \(M/X\) inside \(D\), because \(c\in\cl_M(C-c)\) gives
\[
\rk_{M/X}(D-c)=\rk_{M/X}(D).
\]
If the displayed minimum over \(c\in C\setminus A\) had a unique finite minimizer, its image point in \(M/X\) would be a unique finite minimizer on such a circuit, contradicting \(u\in\Trop(M/X)\).  The quotient criterion proves \(\Trop(p^\dagger)\subseteq\Trop(M)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Involution and flat quotients]\label{lem:invflat}
For every valuated quotient \(p\), \((p^\dagger)^\dagger=p\).  If \(p^F\) denotes the constant valuated matroid of \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\), then
\[
(p^F)^\dagger=p^{F^\perp}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(p\) have rank \(k\), and let \(n=r-k\).  If \(I\in\binomE k\) is \(M\)-dependent, then both \(p_I\) and \((p^\dagger)^\dagger_I\) are \(\infty\).  If \(I\) is independent and \(F=\cl_M(I)\), then
\[
(p^\dagger)^\dagger_I=\overline{p^\dagger}(F^\perp).
\]
Choose an \(M\)-basis \(J\) of \(F^\perp\).  Then
\[
\overline{p^\dagger}(F^\perp)=p^\dagger_J
=\bar p(\cl_M(J)^\perp)=\bar p((F^\perp)^\perp)=\bar p(F)=p_I.
\]

For the flat quotient, let \(f=\rk(F)\).  A rank \(r-f\) flat \(G\) satisfies \(\bar p^F(G)<\infty\) iff \(G\vee F=E\).  Since \(\rk(G)+\rk(F)=r\) and \(M\) is modular, this is equivalent to \(G\wedge F=\varnothing\), i.e. \(G\) is a lattice complement of \(F\).  The anti-involution sends complements of \(F\) to complements of \(F^\perp\), because it interchanges meets and joins and sends \(\varnothing\) to \(E\).  Therefore the dagger support and values of \(p^F\) are exactly those of \(p^{F^\perp}\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Annihilator formula]\label{lem:annihilator}
Let \(p\) be a valuated quotient of the simple matroid \(M\).  For \(x\in\Trop(M)\), regard \(x\) as a rank-one valuated quotient and form \(x^\dagger\).  Then
\[
x\in \Trop(p^\dagger)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(x^\dagger).
\tag{\(*\)}
\]
Consequently \(p^\dagger\) depends only on the tropical linear space \(\Trop(p)\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(B=\{b_1,\ldots,b_r\}\) be an \(M\)-basis and define its polar basis by
\[
b_i^*=\cl_M(B-b_i)^\perp.
\]
Because \(M\) is simple, \(b_i^*\) is a single element.  For \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\),
\[
\cl_M\{b_i^*:i\in S\}
=
\cl_M\{b_i:i\notin S\}^{\perp},
\]
since joins are changed to meets by \(\perp\), and the flats spanned by subsets of \(B\) form a Boolean lattice.  Hence \(B^*=\{b_1^*,\ldots,b_r^*\}\) is a basis and \((B^*)^*=B\).

Let \(p\) have rank \(k\).  Define a rank \(k\) valuated matroid \(\mu_B\) on \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\) by
\[
\mu_B(T)=p_{\{b_i:i\in T\}}.
\]
It has rank \(k\), because \(\supp(p)\) is a quotient of \(M\), so every \(M\)-basis spans \(N=\supp(p)\).  For \(|S|=r-k\),
\[
p^\dagger_{\{b_i^*:i\in S\}}
=
\bar p\!\left(\cl_M\{b_i^*:i\in S\}^{\perp}\right)
=
\bar p\!\left(\cl_M\{b_i:i\notin S\}\right)
=
\mu_B(\{1,\ldots,r\}\setminus S).
\]
Thus \(p^\dagger|_{B^*}=\mu_B^*\).

We use the standard tropical annihilator identity: for a valuated matroid \(\mu\) on \(Q\) and \(u\in\T^Q\),
\[
u\in\Trop(\mu^*)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Trop(\mu)\subseteq H_u,
\]
where \(H_u=\{y:\min_i(u_i+y_i)\text{ has no unique finite minimizer}\}\).  Indeed, the circuits of \(\mu^*\) are the cocircuits of \(\mu\), and \(\Trop(\mu)\) is the tropical convex hull of the cocircuits, while \(H_u\) is tropically convex.

Assume first that \(x\in\Trop(p^\dagger)\).  Fix \(B\) and put \(u_B=(x_{b_1^*},\ldots,x_{b_r^*})\).  Since \(p^\dagger|_{B^*}=\mu_B^*\), we have \(u_B\in\Trop(\mu_B^*)\), hence \(\Trop(\mu_B)\subseteq H_{u_B}\).  If \(y\in\Trop(p)\), then \(y|_B\in\Trop(\mu_B)\), unless all its coordinates are \(\infty\), in which case the following condition is automatic.  Therefore
\[
\min_i(y_{b_i}+x_{b_i^*})
\]
has no unique finite minimizer.  But for the rank \(r-1\) quotient \(x^\dagger\),
\[
(x^\dagger)_{B-b_i}=x_{b_i^*}.
\]
Thus the defining equation for \(y\in\Trop(x^\dagger)\) holds on every \(M\)-basis \(B\).

It remains only to check dependent \(r\)-sets \(K\).  If \(\rk_M(K)\le r-2\), all \((r-1)\)-subsets \(K-e\) are dependent and all terms are \(\infty\).  If \(\rk_M(K)=r-1\), then \(K\) has a unique \(M\)-circuit \(D\).  The finite terms occur exactly for \(e\in D\), and \(\cl_M(K-e)\) is the same hyperplane for all such \(e\); hence the equation reduces, up to adding a common constant, to the circuit equation for \(D\), which holds because \(y\in\Trop(M)\).  Thus \(y\in\Trop(x^\dagger)\), and \(\Trop(p)\subseteq\Trop(x^\dagger)\).

Conversely assume \(\Trop(p)\subseteq\Trop(x^\dagger)\).  Fix \(B\) and \(u_B\).  By the annihilator identity, it suffices to show that each cocircuit of \(\mu_B\) lies in \(H_{u_B}\).  Such a cocircuit has the form \(i\mapsto p_{A\cup b_i}\), where \(A=\{b_i:i\in S\}\) and \(|S|=k-1\).  It is the restriction to \(B\) of the valuated cocircuit \(e\mapsto p_{A\cup e}\) of \(p\).  If this vector is identically \(\infty\), there is nothing to prove; otherwise it is a point of \(\Trop(p)\), hence of \(\Trop(x^\dagger)\).  Testing the defining equation of \(\Trop(x^\dagger)\) on the basis \(B\) gives
\[
\min_i(p_{A\cup b_i}+x_{b_i^*})
\]
with no unique finite minimizer.  Thus \(u_B\in\Trop(\mu_B^*)\).

Since \(B\mapsto B^*\) is a bijection on \(M\)-bases, the previous paragraph says that \(x\) satisfies the defining equations of \(p^\dagger\) on every Boolean apartment coming from an \(M\)-basis.  Let \(J\in\binomE{n+1}\), where \(n=\rk(p^\dagger)\).  If \(J\) is independent, extend it to an \(M\)-basis and use the apartment calculation.  If \(\rk_M(J)\le n-1\), all \(n\)-subsets \(J-j\) are dependent.  If \(\rk_M(J)=n\), then \(J\) has a unique circuit \(D\); the finite coefficients \(p^\dagger_{J-j}\) occur exactly for \(j\in D\), and for those \(j\) the flats \(\cl_M(J-j)\) are equal.  The equation is therefore the circuit equation for \(D\), satisfied by \(x\in\Trop(M)\).  Hence \(x\in\Trop(p^\dagger)\).

Thus \((*)\) holds, and the right-hand side depends only on \(\Trop(p)\).  Therefore so does \(\Trop(p^\dagger)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The theorem for simple matroids]\label{prop:simple}
Theorem \ref{thm:main} holds when \(M\) is simple.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If \(r=0\), the assertion is immediate.  Otherwise, for \(X\in\Dr(M)\), choose a valuated quotient \(p\) with \(X=\Trop(p)\) and define
\[
\Phi(X)=\Trop(p^\dagger).
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:annihilator}, this is independent of the chosen \(p\).  Lemma \ref{lem:invflat} gives \(\Phi^2=\operatorname{id}\).  If \(X\subseteq Y\) and \(x\in\Phi(Y)\), then by Lemma \ref{lem:annihilator},
\[
Y\subseteq\Trop(x^\dagger).
\]
Hence \(X\subseteq\Trop(x^\dagger)\), so \(x\in\Phi(X)\).  Thus \(\Phi(Y)\subseteq\Phi(X)\), and \(\Phi\) is order-reversing.  Finally Lemma \ref{lem:invflat} gives
\[
\Phi\!\left(\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})\right)
=
\Trop(M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp})
\]
for every flat \(F\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:main}]
Let \(S=\operatorname{si}(M)\).  By Lemma \ref{lem:simplification}, \(\Delta:\Dr(S)\to\Dr(M)\) is a poset isomorphism.  The flat-lattice anti-involution on \(\cL(M)\cong\cL(S)\) induces one on \(\cL(S)\).  By Proposition \ref{prop:simple}, there is an order-reversing involution
\[
\Phi_S:\Dr(S)\to\Dr(S)
\]
extending the induced involution on flats.  Define \(\Phi_M:\Dr(M)\to\Dr(M)\) by
\[
\Phi_M(\Delta(X))=\Delta(\Phi_S(X)).
\]
Because \(\Delta\) is a poset isomorphism, \(\Phi_M\) is an order-reversing involution.

If \(F\in\cL(M)\) corresponds to \(\bar F\in\cL(S)\), then \(F^\perp\) corresponds to \(\bar F^\perp\), and Lemma \ref{lem:simplification} gives
\[
\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})
=
\Delta\bigl(\Trop(S/\bar F\oplus U_{0,\bar F})\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_M\!\left(\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})\right)
&=
\Delta\!\left(\Phi_S\!\left(\Trop(S/\bar F\oplus U_{0,\bar F})\right)\right)\\
&=
\Delta\!\left(\Trop(S/\bar F^\perp\oplus U_{0,\bar F^\perp})\right)\\
&=
\Trop(M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}),
\end{aligned}
\]
as required.
\end{proof}

\title{Submission C solution to Problem 8}
\date{}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We prove that if the lattice of flats of a finite matroid \(M\) admits an order-reversing involution \(F\mapsto F^\perp\), then the relative Dressian
\[
   \Dr(M)=\{\text{tropical linear subspaces of }\Trop(M)\}
\]
admits an order-reversing involution extending \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) under the natural embedding
\[
   \cL(M)^{\operatorname{op}}\hookrightarrow \Dr(M),\qquad
   F\longmapsto \Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}).
\]
The main point is that an order-reversing involution of a geometric lattice forces the lattice to be modular.  For modular matroids, valuated quotients are naturally valuated matroids on the modular lattice of flats, and the desired involution is obtained by pulling back along the lattice polarity.
\end{abstract}

\section{Conventions and background}

Let \(M\) be a finite matroid of rank \(d\) on ground set \(E\).  We write
\[
  \cL(M)
\]
for its lattice of flats, ordered by inclusion.  If \(F\in \cL(M)\), then
\[
  X_F:=\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})
\]
is a tropical linear subspace of \(\Trop(M)\).  The assignment \(F\mapsto X_F\) is order-reversing, hence gives an embedding
\[
   \cL(M)^{\operatorname{op}}\hookrightarrow \Dr(M).
\]

We use the valuated-matroid model of tropical linear spaces.  A valuated matroid \(p\) of rank \(s\) on \(E\) determines a tropical linear space \(\Trop(p)\) of dimension \(s-1\), and tropical linear spaces are identified up to adding a global scalar to \(p\).  If \(q\) and \(p\) are valuated matroids of ranks \(t\ge s\), then
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q)
\]
if and only if \(p\) is a valuated quotient of \(q\), equivalently \((q,p)\) satisfies the tropical incidence--Plucker relations.  This is the valuated flag matroid correspondence; see Speyer \cite{SpeyerTLS}, Maclagan--Sturmfels \cite[Ch.~4]{MS}, and Brandt--Eur--Zhang \cite{BEZ}.

For a flat \(F\), the corresponding valuated quotient \(p_F\) of rank \(d-\rk(F)\) is the trivial valuation on the matroid \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\).  Thus, if \(B\subseteq E\) has size \(d-\rk(F)\), then
\[
   p_F(B)=
   \begin{cases}
   0, & \text{if } B \text{ is a basis of }M/F,\\
   \infty, & \text{otherwise}.
   \end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, for an independent set \(B\) of \(M\),
\[
   p_F(B)<\infty
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \cl_M(B)\vee F=E.
\]

\section{A lattice-theoretic consequence of polarity}

We first record the key structural consequence of the existence of an order-reversing involution on the lattice of flats.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:selfdual-implies-modular}
Let \(L\) be a finite ranked semimodular lattice of rank \(d\).  Suppose that \(L\) admits an order-reversing involution
\[
   \alpha:L\longrightarrow L,\qquad x\longmapsto x^\perp .
\]
Then \(L\) is modular.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(\alpha\) is an order-reversing involution, it sends maximal chains to maximal chains with the order reversed.  Hence
\[
   \rk(x^\perp)=d-\rk(x)
\]
for all \(x\in L\).

Because \(L\) is semimodular, for all \(x,y\in L\) we have
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)\ge \rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
Apply semimodularity to \(x^\perp\) and \(y^\perp\).  Using
\[
   x^\perp\wedge y^\perp=(x\vee y)^\perp,
   \qquad
   x^\perp\vee y^\perp=(x\wedge y)^\perp,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \rk(x^\perp)+\rk(y^\perp)
  &\ge
  \rk((x\vee y)^\perp)+\rk((x\wedge y)^\perp)\\
  (d-\rk(x))+(d-\rk(y))
  &\ge
  (d-\rk(x\vee y))+(d-\rk(x\wedge y)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Cancelling \(2d\) gives
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)\le \rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
Together with semimodularity, equality holds:
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)=\rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
This is precisely the rank form of modularity.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:M-modular}
If \(M\) admits an order-reversing involution on \(\cL(M)\), then \(\cL(M)\) is modular.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The lattice of flats of a matroid is a finite geometric lattice, hence finite, ranked, atomic, and semimodular.  Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:selfdual-implies-modular}.
\end{proof}

\section{Valuated quotients of modular matroids}

We now use the standard modular-lattice form of valuated matroids.

Let \(M\) be modular of rank \(d\).  For \(0\le s\le d\), write
\[
   \cL_s(M):=\{F\in \cL(M):\rk(F)=s\}.
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:flat-invariance}
Let \(p\) be a rank-\(s\) valuated quotient of the trivial valuated matroid of \(M\).  If \(B,B'\subseteq E\) are bases of the same rank-\(s\) flat of \(M\), then
\[
   p(B)=p(B').
\]
Hence \(p\) descends to a function
\[
   \bar p:\cL_s(M)\longrightarrow \mathbb T,\qquad
   \bar p(F)=p(B)
\]
for any basis \(B\) of \(F\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
It is enough to prove the claim when \(B\) and \(B'\) differ by one element.  Let
\[
   B=S\cup\{i\},\qquad B'=S\cup\{j\},
\]
where \(|S|=s-1\), and assume
\[
   \cl_M(S\cup\{i\})=\cl_M(S\cup\{j\})=:F.
\]
Extend \(S\cup\{i\}\), equivalently \(S\cup\{j\}\), to a basis of \(M\) by choosing a set \(C\) of size \(d-s\) such that
\[
   S\cup\{i\}\cup C
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   S\cup\{j\}\cup C
\]
are both bases of \(M\).

Let
\[
   J:=S\cup\{i,j\}\cup C.
\]
Then \(|J|=d+1\).  Consider the tropical incidence relation for the valuated quotient \(p\), indexed by \(S\) and \(J\):
\[
   \min_{e\in J\setminus S}\{p(S\cup\{e\})+\mu(J\setminus\{e\})\}
\]
must attain its minimum at least twice, where \(\mu\) is the trivial valuation of \(M\).  For \(e=i\) and \(e=j\), the terms are respectively
\[
   p(S\cup\{i\})+\mu(S\cup\{j\}\cup C)=p(B),
\]
and
\[
   p(S\cup\{j\})+\mu(S\cup\{i\}\cup C)=p(B').
\]
For \(e\in C\), the set
\[
   J\setminus\{e\}=S\cup\{i,j\}\cup(C\setminus\{e\})
\]
is dependent in \(M\), because \(i\) and \(j\) are dependent over \(S\).  Hence
\[
   \mu(J\setminus\{e\})=\infty.
\]
Thus the incidence relation reduces to saying that the minimum of the two values \(p(B)\) and \(p(B')\) is attained twice.  Therefore \(p(B)=p(B')\).

Since the basis graph of a matroid restriction \(M|F\) is connected, any two bases of \(F\) are connected by such single-element exchanges.  The result follows.
\end{proof}

We will use the following standard form of valuated matroid duality on modular geometric lattices.  It is the modular-lattice version of ordinary valuated-matroid duality.  In the Boolean case it is exactly the usual operation
\[
   p^*(A)=p(E\setminus A).
\]
For modular lattices, the same construction is obtained by replacing set-complement by the lattice anti-isomorphism.  See Dress--Wenzel \cite{DW}, Murota \cite[Ch.~4]{Murota}, and the flag version in Brandt--Eur--Zhang \cite{BEZ}.

\begin{theorem}[Modular-lattice valuated duality]\label{thm:modular-duality}
Let \(M\) be a modular matroid of rank \(d\), and let
\[
   \alpha:\cL(M)\longrightarrow \cL(M),\qquad F\longmapsto F^\perp
\]
be an order-reversing involution.  Let \(p\) be a rank-\(s\) valuated quotient of \(M\), and let \(\bar p:\cL_s(M)\to \mathbb T\) be the descended function from Lemma~\ref{lem:flat-invariance}.  Define a function
\[
   \bar p^{\,\perp}:\cL_{d-s}(M)\longrightarrow \mathbb T
\]
by
\[
   \bar p^{\,\perp}(G):=\bar p(G^\perp).
\]
Then \(\bar p^{\,\perp}\) is the flat-valued form of a rank-\((d-s)\) valuated quotient \(p^\perp\) of \(M\).

Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \((p^\perp)^\perp=p\) up to tropical scalar;
\item if \(q\) and \(p\) are valuated quotients of \(M\) with \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\), then
\[
   p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp;
\]
\item the construction is compatible with tropical linear spaces:
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q)
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \Trop(q^\perp)\subseteq \Trop(p^\perp).
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We recall the argument.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:flat-invariance}, every valuated quotient \(p\) of a modular matroid \(M\) is equivalently a valuated matroid on the modular lattice \(\cL(M)\), with coordinates indexed by rank-\(s\) flats.  The tropical Plucker relations are local relations in length-four intervals of \(\cL(M)\), and the tropical incidence relations for a pair of quotients are the corresponding local flag-Plucker relations.  An order-reversing lattice isomorphism sends length-four intervals to length-four intervals and interchanges rank \(s\) with rank \(d-s\).  Therefore pulling the flat-valued Plucker coordinates back along \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) preserves the tropical Plucker relations and reverses the flag incidence relations.

Thus \(\bar p^\perp\) is again a valuated quotient of \(M\), now of rank \(d-s\).  Since \(\perp\) is an involution on \(\cL(M)\), applying the construction twice gives back \(\bar p\).  Finally, the valuated flag relation \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\) is carried to \(p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp\), which is precisely the asserted reversal of containment of tropical linear spaces.
\end{proof}

\section{Construction of the involution}

Let \(L=\Trop(p)\in \Dr(M)\), where \(p\) is a valuated quotient of \(M\) of rank \(s\).  Define
\[
   \Phi(L):=\Trop(p^\perp),
\]
where \(p^\perp\) is the rank-\((d-s)\) quotient supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality}.

Equivalently, if \(A\subseteq E\) is independent of size \(d-s\), then
\[
   p^\perp(A)=\bar p(\cl_M(A)^\perp),
\]
and if \(A\) is dependent in \(M\), then \(p^\perp(A)=\infty\).

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid whose lattice of flats admits an order-reversing involution
\[
   F\longmapsto F^\perp.
\]
Then the map
\[
   \Phi:\Dr(M)\longrightarrow \Dr(M),\qquad
   \Trop(p)\longmapsto \Trop(p^\perp),
\]
is an order-reversing involution.  Moreover, for every flat \(F\in \cL(M)\),
\[
   \Phi\!\left(\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})\right)
   =
   \Trop(M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}).
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) extends the given involution \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) on \(\cL(M)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:M-modular}, \(M\) is modular.  Hence Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality} applies.

First, \(\Phi\) is well-defined because tropical linear spaces are identified with valuated matroids up to tropical scalar, and the construction \(p\mapsto p^\perp\) is unchanged by adding a global scalar to \(p\).

Second, since \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) is an involution on \(\cL(M)\), Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality} gives
\[
   (p^\perp)^\perp=p
\]
up to tropical scalar.  Therefore
\[
   \Phi^2=\operatorname{id}_{\Dr(M)}.
\]

Third, suppose
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q).
\]
Equivalently, \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\).  By Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality},
\[
   p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp.
\]
Therefore
\[
   \Trop(q^\perp)\subseteq \Trop(p^\perp),
\]
which is precisely
\[
   \Phi(\Trop(q))\subseteq \Phi(\Trop(p)).
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) is order-reversing.

It remains to check that \(\Phi\) extends the given flat involution.  Let \(F\in\cL(M)\), and put \(f=\rk(F)\).  Let \(p_F\) be the trivial valuation of the quotient \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\), so \(p_F\) has rank \(d-f\).  In flat-valued form,
\[
   \bar p_F(H)=
   \begin{cases}
   0, & H\vee F=E,\\
   \infty, & H\vee F\ne E,
   \end{cases}
   \qquad H\in \cL_{d-f}(M).
\]
Let \(G\in\cL_f(M)\).  Then
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)
   =
   \bar p_F(G^\perp).
\]
Thus
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)=0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G^\perp\vee F=E.
\]
Applying the order-reversing involution gives
\[
   G^\perp\vee F=E
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G\wedge F^\perp=\hat 0.
\]
Because \(\cL(M)\) is modular and
\[
   \rk(G)+\rk(F^\perp)=f+(d-f)=d,
\]
the condition \(G\wedge F^\perp=\hat 0\) is equivalent to
\[
   G\vee F^\perp=E.
\]
Therefore
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)=0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G\vee F^\perp=E.
\]
But this is exactly the flat-valued trivial valuation of the quotient
\[
   M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}.
\]
Hence
\[
   p_F^\perp=p_{F^\perp},
\]
and consequently
\[
   \Phi(X_F)=X_{F^\perp}.
\]
This proves the claimed extension property.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The answer to the question is affirmative: every order-reversing involution on \(\cL(M)\) extends to an order-reversing involution on \(\Dr(M)\).
\end{corollary}

\title{Submission A solution to Problem 10}
\date{}
\maketitle


\section*{Problem statement and interpretation}

Irreducible means not a non-trivial graph join; equivalently the complement
graph \(\Gamma^c\) is connected.  All traces are faithful normal traces.  For
\(U\subset V\), \(M_U\) denotes the graph product over the induced subgraph and
\(E_U:M\to M_U\) its canonical trace-preserving expectation.

We use the notation of Ding--Kunnawalkam Elayavalli--Peterson \cite{DKEP}.
For a finite algebra \(N\), put \(A_N=\mathbb B(L^2N)\) and
\[
        \cA_N=(A_N^{\sharp_J})^*,
\]
where \(\sharp_J\) means simultaneous normality for the \(N\)- and
\(JNJ\)-bimodule structures.  If \(X\) is an \(N\)-boundary piece, \(K_X(N)\)
is DKEP's compact hereditary algebra and \(q_X\in\cA_N\) is the support of
\((K_X(N)^{\sharp_J})^*\).  For \(X=\mathbb K(L^2N)\) write \(q_0\).  Set
\[
 \widetilde S_X(N)=\{T\in\cA_N:[T,a]\in q_X\cA_Nq_X\hbox{ for all }
 a\in JNJ\}.
\]
For a separable finite factor, DKEP Lemma 8.5 says that proper proximality
relative to \(X\) is equivalent to the absence of an \(N\)-central state on
\(\widetilde S_X(N)\) whose restriction to \(N\) is the trace.  Equivalently
one may rule out \(N\)-central states whose restriction is normal, since a
normal central state on a finite factor is the trace after normalization.

For a bounded vector \(\xi\) in an \(M\)-\(N\) correspondence, \(T_\xi\) denotes
DKEP's coefficient operator \(L^2M\to L^2N\); if \(\eta\) is bounded in an
\(N\)-\(P\) correspondence, then
\[
        T_{\xi\otimes_N\eta}=T_\eta T_\xi,\qquad
        T_{\bar\xi}=T_\xi^* .                                    \tag{1}
\]

\section*{Boundary supports and coefficients}

We use DKEP's ordinary-bidual realization of the normal bidual.  Thus
\(\cA_N\) is viewed as a von Neumann subalgebra of \(A_N^{**}\); its unit is
denoted by \(p_N\).  Products of support projections are computed inside the
honest von Neumann algebra \(A_N^{**}\), not by multiplying the
non-multiplicative canonical images of concrete operators.

\begin{lemma}[ordinary support bookkeeping]\label{lem:support}
Let \(Y\subset A_N\) be a hereditary \(C^*\)-subalgebra invariant under the
multiplier actions of \(N\) and \(JNJ\), and assume that the induced
representations \(N,JNJ\to M(Y)\) are faithful.  Let \(r_Y\in A_N^{**}\) be
the ordinary open support projection of \(Y\).  Then \(r_Y\) commutes with
\(p_N\), and the support in \(\cA_N\) of the included corner
\((Y^{\sharp_J})^*\) is \(p_Nr_Y\).  Every contractive approximate unit of
\(Y\) converges weak* in \(A_N^{**}\) to \(r_Y\).

If \(X\) is one of the boundary pieces used below and \(\rho_X\) denotes the
ordinary support of \(K_X(N)\), while \(r_X\) denotes the ordinary support of
\(X\), then
\[
        q_X=p_Nr_X=p_N\rho_X .                                    \tag{2}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(p_\ell\) and \(p_r\) be DKEP's one-normal support projections in
\(A_N^{**}\), for the \(N\)- and \(JNJ\)-module structures respectively.  In
the one-normal construction \(p_\ell\in N^{**}\) and
\(p_r\in (JNJ)^{**}\).  Since the concrete algebras \(N\) and \(JNJ\) commute
in \(A_N\), their bidual images commute in \(A_N^{**}\): approximate elements
of the biduals weak* by bounded nets from the concrete algebras and use
separate weak* continuity of multiplication.  Hence \(p_\ell p_r=p_rp_\ell\).

The one-normal support paragraph preceding DKEP Remark 2.8 identifies
\((A_N^{\sharp_N})^*=p_\ell A_N^{**}p_\ell\) and
\((A_N^{\sharp_{JNJ}})^*=p_rA_N^{**}p_r\).  DKEP Proposition 2.10 identifies
the simultaneous normal bidual with their intersection inside \(A_N^{**}\).
For commuting projections \(e,f\) in a von Neumann algebra,
\(eRe\cap fRf=(ef)R(ef)\); therefore
\[
        \cA_N=(A_N^{\sharp_J})^*=p_NA_N^{**}p_N,\qquad
        p_N=p_\ell p_r .                                          \tag{3}
\]

Apply the same one-normal support statement to \(Y\) for each of the two
normal structures.  The faithfulness hypothesis is exactly the hypothesis
needed there for the multiplier actions on \(Y\).  Thus \(r_Y\) commutes with
both \(p_\ell\) and \(p_r\), and the two one-normal biduals of \(Y\) are
\(r_Yp_\ell A_N^{**}p_\ell r_Y\) and \(r_Yp_rA_N^{**}p_rr_Y\).  Applying
Proposition 2.10 to the inclusion \(Y\subset A_N\) and using the elementary
intersection formula once more gives
\[
        (Y^{\sharp_J})^*
        = r_Yp_NA_N^{**}p_Nr_Y
        = (p_Nr_Y)\,\cA_N\,(p_Nr_Y).
\]
Thus its support projection in \(\cA_N\) is \(p_Nr_Y\).  The weak* convergence
of approximate units to \(r_Y\) is the usual open-support property in the
ordinary bidual.

It remains to compare \(X\) with \(K_X(N)\).  For the subalgebra boundary
pieces used below the faithfulness assumption is automatic: if, for example,
\(a e_B=0\), then \(E_B(a^*a)=0\), hence \(a=0\), and the right action is
similar; the same holds for \(K_X(N)\) since \(K(L^2N)\subset X\subset K_X(N)\).
By the first part, the normal supports of \(X\) and \(K_X(N)\) are \(p_Nr_X\)
and \(p_N\rho_X\).  We show that their simultaneous-normal annihilators
coincide.

Let \(\phi\in A_N^{\sharp_J}\) vanish on \(X\).  DKEP Proposition 3.6 gives
\(K_X(N)\subset K_X^{\infty,1}(N)\), where \(K_X^{\infty,1}(N)\) is the
\(\|\cdot\|_{\infty,1}\)-closure of \(X\).  DKEP Theorem 5.6, applied with the
same boundary piece on both sides, says that every
\(T\in K_X^{\infty,1}(N)\) is killed by every simultaneous-normal functional
which vanishes on \(X A_N X\).  Since \(X\) is hereditary, \(X A_N X\subset X\);
hence \(\phi(T)=0\) for all \(T\in K_X(N)\).  The reverse annihilator inclusion
is immediate from \(X\subset K_X(N)\), which is part of DKEP's construction.
Equal preannihilators give the same weak* closed corner in \(\cA_N\), hence the
same support projection.  Since \(q_X\) is by definition the support of
\((K_X(N)^{\sharp_J})^*\), (2) follows.
\end{proof}

For an expected inclusion \(B\subset N\), put \(H={}_NL^2N_B\) and
\[
        \cH_B=H\otimes_B\overline H
             ={}_NL^2N_B\otimes_B{}_BL^2N_N .
\]
Let \(\mathcal E_B=\{T_{\eta\otimes_B\bar\xi}:\xi,\eta\in H_{\rm b}\}\).

\begin{lemma}[subalgebra fusion]\label{lem:subalg}
The boundary piece \(X_B\) is hereditarily generated by the positive
operators \(s^*s\), \(s\in\mathcal E_B\), equivalently by
\(T_\alpha^*T_\alpha\) with \(\alpha\) an elementary bounded tensor in
\(\cH_B\).  Moreover \(\cH_B\cong\overline{\cH_B}\), and every coefficient
operator \(T_\alpha\) of a bounded vector in any Hilbert direct sum of copies
of \(\cH_B\) belongs to \(K_{X_B}(N)\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
DKEP Example 5.11 applied to \(H={}_NL^2N_B\) says that \(X_B\) is the
hereditary algebra generated by \(T_\xi^*T_\eta\), \(\xi,\eta\in H_{\rm b}\).
By (1), \(T_{\eta\otimes_B\bar\xi}=T_{\bar\xi}T_\eta=T_\xi^*T_\eta\).

Let \(Y\) be the hereditary algebra generated by \(\{s^*s:s\in\mathcal E_B\}\).
Since \(\mathcal E_B\) is self-adjoint, \(Y\) contains \(s^*s\) and \(ss^*\).
If \(r\) is the ordinary support of \(Y\), then
\((1-r)s^*s(1-r)=0\) and \((1-r)ss^*(1-r)=0\); hence \((1-r)s=s(1-r)=0\).
Thus \(s=rsr\in rA_N^{**}r\cap A_N=Y\).  So all generators
\(T_\xi^*T_\eta\) of \(X_B\) lie in \(Y\), and the reverse inclusion is
immediate.

The conjugation \(\overline{\xi\otimes_B\bar\eta}\mapsto
\eta\otimes_B\bar\xi\) gives \(\overline{\cH_B}\cong\cH_B\).  Let
\(\mathcal C\) be the elementary bounded tensors in \(\cH_B\).  They are
\(N\)-\(N\) cyclic, and \(T_\alpha\in X_B\subset X_BA_NX_B\) for
\(\alpha\in\mathcal C\).  Hence DKEP Theorem 5.10(1) applies, so \(\cH_B\) is
mixing relative to \(X_B\times X_B\).  For a Hilbert direct sum
\(\bigoplus_{j\in J}\cH_B\), take the vectors of \(\mathcal C\) placed in one
summand.  Their \(N\)-\(N\) span contains the finite-support algebraic direct
sum, hence is dense, and the coefficient operator of such a one-summand vector
is exactly the coefficient operator above (zero against the other summands).
Thus Theorem 5.10(1) holds for the whole direct sum.  Theorem 5.10(3), followed
by Proposition 5.9, gives \(T_\alpha\in K_{X_B,X_B}(N,N)=K_{X_B}(N)A_N
K_{X_B}(N)\subset K_{X_B}(N)\) for every bounded vector \(\alpha\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[finite fusion calculus]\label{lem:fusion}
Let \(X\) be a boundary piece for \(N\), with \(N,JNJ\subset M(X)\).  Finite
Connes fusions, conjugates, and Hilbert direct sums of \(N\)-\(N\)
correspondences which are mixing relative to \(X\times X\) are again mixing
relative to \(X\times X\).  Consequently, if \(K\) is any such finite-fusion
correspondence and \(\xi\in K\) is bounded, then \(T_\xi\in K_X(N)\).

For \(U\subset V\), put \(H_U=L^2M\otimes_{M_U}L^2M\).  Let \(\cT_U\) be the
linear span of all \(T_\xi\), where \(\xi\) is a bounded vector in a finite
direct sum of non-empty finite fusions of \(H_U\) and \(\overline{H_U}\).
Then \(\cT_U\) is a \(*\)-algebra, and \(X_{M_U}\) has a contractive
approximate unit in the norm closure of \(\{t^*t:t\in\cT_U\}\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a mixing correspondence \(H\), Theorem 5.10 says that
\[
  \mathcal C_H=\{\xi\in H_{\rm b}: T_\xi\in X A_N X\}
\]
is \(N\)-\(N\) cyclic.  Direct sums are handled by placing the cyclic vectors
in one summand; their span contains the finite-support algebraic sum and is
dense, while the coefficient condition is unchanged.  If \(H\) and \(K\) are
mixing and \(\xi\in\mathcal C_H,\eta\in\mathcal C_K\), then \(\xi\otimes_N\eta\)
is bounded, such elementary tensors are cyclic for \(H\otimes_NK\), and
\[
        T_{\xi\otimes\eta}=T_\eta T_\xi\in (X A_N X)(X A_N X)\subset X A_N X,
\]
because \(X\) is hereditary.  Thus the cyclic-vector criterion proves mixing
for fusions.  For the conjugate correspondence, the cyclic vectors are
\(\bar\xi\) and \(T_{\bar\xi}=T_\xi^*\in X A_NX\).  Iterating gives the first
assertion.  Applying Theorem 5.10(3) and Proposition 5.9 to any bounded vector
\(\xi\) in such a correspondence gives
\[
        T_\xi\in K_{X,X}(N,N)=K_X(N)A_NK_X(N)\subset K_X(N).
\]

The algebra property of \(\cT_U\) follows term by term from (1) with the order
convention \(T_\eta T_\xi=T_{\xi\otimes\eta}\): the product of two coefficient
operators is the coefficient of the corresponding fused bounded vector, and the
adjoint is the coefficient of the conjugate vector.  Since \(\cT_U\) is defined
as a linear span, this proves closure under products and adjoints.  By Lemma
\ref{lem:subalg}, \(X_{M_U}\) is hereditarily generated
by \(T_\xi^*T_\xi\) for elementary tensors in \(H_U\), and these \(T_\xi\)'s
belong to \(\cT_U\).  If \(s\) is a finite positive sum of such generators,
then \(g_\varepsilon(s)=s(s+\varepsilon)^{-1}\) is in the hereditary algebra
generated by the summands.  Polynomials in \(s\) with zero constant term
approximate \(g_\varepsilon(s)^{1/2}\), so \(g_\varepsilon(s)\) lies in the
norm closure of \(\{t^*t:t\in\cT_U\}\).  The usual net over \(s\) and
\(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) is a contractive approximate unit.
\end{proof}

If \(Z\subset U\), then \(e_{M_Z}\le e_{M_U}\); hence
\(X_{M_Z}\subset X_{M_U}\) and \(K_{X_{M_Z}}(M)\subset K_{X_{M_U}}(M)\).

\begin{lemma}[intersection of boundary supports]\label{lem:intersection}
Let \(q_U=q_{X_{M_U}}\).  For \(U,W\subset V\), with \(I=U\cap W\),
\[
        0\le q_Wq_Uq_W\le q_I .
\]
Consequently, if \(I=\cap_{i=1}^m U_i\), then
\[
q_{U_m}q_{U_{m-1}}\cdots q_{U_1}q_{U_2}\cdots q_{U_{m-1}}q_{U_m}
   \in q_I\cA_Mq_I .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The graph-product bimodule decomposition and fusion rule of
\cite[Theorem 5.4 and Proposition 5.5]{CDHJKN} give
\[
        H_A\otimes_M H_B\cong
        \bigoplus_{C\subset A\cap B}H_C^{\oplus m(A,B,C)} .        \tag{3}
\]
Since \(H_A\cong\overline{H_A}\), induction shows that a finite fusion whose
labels are \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\) decomposes into a direct sum of \(H_C\)'s with
\(C\subset A_1\cap\cdots\cap A_n\).  The implementing unitary is
\(M\)-bimodular, so bounded vectors remain bounded.

Let \(\mathcal P_R\) be the norm closure of \(\{t^*t:t\in\cT_R\}\).  We claim
that
\[
        a\,b\,c\in K_{X_{M_I}}(M)             \tag{4}
\]
whenever \(a,c\in\mathcal P_W\) and \(b\in\mathcal P_U\).  It is enough to
consider \(a=t_1^*t_1\), \(b=s^*s\), \(c=t_2^*t_2\).  Write
\(t_j\) and \(s\) as finite sums of coefficient operators.  A summand in the
expansion of \(t_1^*t_1s^*st_2^*t_2\) is
\[
T_{\alpha_1}^*T_{\alpha_2}T_{\beta_1}^*T_{\beta_2}
T_{\alpha_3}^*T_{\alpha_4},
\]
where each \(\alpha_i\) is a bounded vector in a finite direct sum of fusions
with label \(W\), and each \(\beta_i\) is similarly labelled by \(U\).  Replacing
\(T_\alpha^*\) by \(T_{\bar\alpha}\) and using
\(T_\eta T_\xi=T_{\xi\otimes\eta}\), the displayed product is the coefficient
operator of
\[
 \zeta:=\alpha_4\otimes\bar\alpha_3\otimes\beta_2\otimes\bar\beta_1
 \otimes\alpha_2\otimes\bar\alpha_1
\]
(with finite direct sums distributed over the tensor products).  This is a
bounded vector in a finite fusion whose label list contains both \(W\) and
\(U\).  By (3), it is carried by an \(M\)-bimodular unitary to a bounded vector
in a direct sum of \(H_C\)'s with \(C\subset I\); its coefficient operator is
unchanged under this identification.  For each such \(C\), Lemma
\ref{lem:subalg} gives mixing, hence coefficient compactness, relative to
\(X_{M_C}\).  Since \(X_{M_C}\subset X_{M_I}\), the same cyclic vectors are good
for \(X_{M_I}\); the direct-sum argument in Lemma \ref{lem:fusion} therefore
puts the coefficient of the whole direct sum in \(K_{X_{M_I}}(M)\).  Linearity
and norm closure prove (4).

Let \(A=\mathbb B(L^2M)\), let \(p=p_M\) be the unit of \(\cA_M\) in
\(A^{**}\), let \(r_R\) be the ordinary support of \(X_{M_R}\), and let
\(\rho_R\) be the ordinary support of \(K_{X_{M_R}}(M)\).  Lemma
\ref{lem:support} gives
\[
        q_R=pr_R=p\rho_R,\qquad [p,r_R]=[p,\rho_R]=0 .              \tag{5}
\]
Choose contractive approximate units
\(h_\alpha\subset\mathcal P_W\) for \(X_{M_W}\) and
\(k_\beta\subset\mathcal P_U\) for \(X_{M_U}\).  In \(A^{**}\),
\(h_\alpha\to r_W\) and \(k_\beta\to r_U\) weak*.  By (4),
\(h_\alpha k_\beta h_\gamma\in K_{X_{M_I}}(M)\subset
\rho_IA^{**}\rho_I\).  The corner \(\rho_IA^{**}\rho_I\) is weak* closed, and
multiplication in \(A^{**}\) is separately weak* continuous; taking the three
successive limits gives
\[
        r_W r_U r_W\in \rho_I A^{**}\rho_I .
\]
This operator is a positive contraction, hence \(r_Wr_Ur_W\le \rho_I\).
Compressing only now to the simultaneous normal bidual, (5) yields
\[
 q_Wq_Uq_W
 =(pr_Wp)(pr_Up)(pr_Wp)
 =p\,r_Wr_Ur_W\,p
 \le p\rho_Ip=q_I .
\]

The palindromic assertion follows by induction.  If
\(R_{m-1}\le q_{\cap_{i<m}U_i}\), then
\[
q_{U_m}R_{m-1}q_{U_m}
 \le q_{U_m}q_{\cap_{i<m}U_i}q_{U_m}
 \le q_{\cap_iU_i},
\]
using the two-set case for the last inequality.
\end{proof}

\section*{From finitely many relative boundaries to the compact boundary}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:finite}
Let \(N\) be a separable non-amenable finite factor.  Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_m\) be boundary pieces, \(q_i=q_{X_i}\), and suppose
\[
        R:=q_mq_{m-1}\cdots q_1q_2\cdots q_{m-1}q_m\in q_0\cA_Nq_0. \tag{6}
\]
If \(N\) is properly proximal relative to each \(X_i\), then \(N\) is properly
proximal.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Assume not.  DKEP Lemma 8.5 gives an \(N\)-central state \(\omega\) on
\(\widetilde S(N)=\widetilde S_{\mathbb K(L^2N)}(N)\) with
\(\omega|_N=\tau\).  Fix \(i\) and put \(q=q_i\).  Since \(q\) commutes with
\(N\) and \(JNJ\),
\[
 [q^\perp yq^\perp,a]=q^\perp[y,a]q^\perp=0,\qquad a\in JNJ,
\]
for \(y\in\widetilde S_{X_i}(N)\); hence \(q^\perp yq^\perp\in\widetilde
S(N)\).  If \(\omega(q^\perp)>0\), then
\(y\mapsto \omega(q^\perp yq^\perp)/\omega(q^\perp)\) is an \(N\)-central state
on \(\widetilde S_{X_i}(N)\).  On \(N_+\) it is dominated by
\(\omega(q^\perp)^{-1}\tau\), hence is normal; its normalization and centrality
make its restriction the unique normal trace on the factor \(N\), contradicting
relative proper proximality.  Thus \(\omega(q_i^\perp)=0\) for all \(i\).

Each \(q_i\), \(q_0\), and the palindromic product \(R\) commute with \(JNJ\),
so they lie in \(\widetilde S(N)\); their values below are therefore independent
of any extension.  Extend \(\omega\) to a state on the \(C^*\)-algebra
\(\cA_N\) only for the following GNS projection argument; the extension is not
claimed to be \(N\)-central.  In its GNS representation, the equality
\(\omega(q_i^\perp)=0\) implies \(q_i\) fixes the cyclic vector.  Hence
\(\omega(R)=\|(q_1q_2\cdots q_m)\xi_\omega\|^2=1\).  Since \(R\) is a positive
contraction in \(q_0\cA_Nq_0\), \(R\le q_0\), and so \(\omega(q_0)=1\).

DKEP Lemma 8.5 provides the canonical \(N\)- and \(JNJ\)-bimodular u.c.p. map
\[
        \Theta_0:\mathbb B(L^2N)\to q_0\cA_Nq_0,\qquad
        \Theta_0(a)=aq_0\quad(a\in N).
\]
Then \(\psi(T)=\omega(\Theta_0(T))\) is an \(N\)-central state on
\(\mathbb B(L^2N)\).  Since \(q_0\) fixes the GNS cyclic vector,
\(\psi(a)=\omega(aq_0)=\omega(a)=\tau(a)\) for \(a\in N\).  This Connes
hypertrace contradicts non-amenability of \(N\).
\end{proof}

\section*{A relative Bass--Serre paradox}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:BS}
Let \(N=P*_{B}Q\) with trace-preserving expectations and \(Q=B\bbarotimes A\).
Assume that \(A\) has a trace-zero unitary \(a\), and that \(P\) has unitaries
\(w_1,w_2\) satisfying
\[
        E_B(w_i)=0,\qquad E_B(w_1^*w_2)=0 .
\]
Then \(N\) is properly proximal relative to \(X_B\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(H_P=L^2P\ominus L^2B\) and \(H_Q=L^2Q\ominus L^2B\).  The AFP normal form is
\[
 L^2N=L^2B\oplus\!\!\bigoplus_{\substack{n\ge1,\ i_j\in\{P,Q\}\\
 i_j\ne i_{j+1}}}
 H_{i_1}\otimes_B\cdots\otimes_B H_{i_n}.
\]
Let \(p\) and \(q\) project onto the summands whose first letter is \(P\),
respectively \(Q\); then \(1=e_B+p+q\).  Right multiplication by \(B\) preserves
the first letter.  Let \(x\in P\ominus B\).  On \(L^2B\), \(JxJ\) creates a
first-letter \(P\) vector.  On a reduced word with first letter \(Q\), right
multiplication by \(x^*\) either appends or merges at the last letter, but the
first letter remains \(Q\) and no \(L^2B\)-part is created.  On a first-letter
\(P\) word the first letter remains \(P\), except that a length-one word may
produce an \(L^2B\)-component.  Hence
\[
 [p,JxJ]=(1-e_B)JxJe_B-e_BJxJ(1-e_B),\qquad [q,JxJ]=0.             \tag{7}
\]
The symmetric formula holds with \(P,p\) and \(Q,q\) interchanged for
\(x\in Q\ominus B\).  Since \(E_B(x)=0\), \(e_BJxJe_B=0\); hence the two terms
in (7) are just right translates of \(e_B\) (up to sign), so they lie in
\(X_B\subset K_{X_B}^{\infty,1}(N)\).

We now translate DKEP Lemma 6.1.  For a fixed operator \(T\), the set of
\(x\in N\) such that both \([T,JxJ]\) and \([T,Jx^*J]\) lie in
\(K_{X_B}^{\infty,1}(N)\) is a von Neumann algebra; this is Lemma 6.1 applied
to \(B(L^2N)\) with DKEP's right-action convention
\(x\cdot T\cdot y=Jy^*JTJx^*J\).  For \(T=p\) and \(T=q\) this von Neumann
algebra contains \(B\), \(P\ominus B\), and \(Q\ominus B\), hence contains the
von Neumann algebra generated by \(P\) and \(Q\).  Thus \(p,q\in S_{X_B}(N)\).

It remains, by DKEP Theorem 6.2, to rule out an \(N\)-central state
\(\varphi\) on \(S_{X_B}(N)\) with normal restriction to \(N\).  For
\(\eta\in qL^2N\), \(w_i\eta\) is a reduced vector with first letter \(P\).
Moreover \(q\,w_1^*w_2\,q=0\): if a reduced vector begins with \(Q\), left
multiplication by the centered \(P\)-letter \(w_1^*w_2\) produces a vector
beginning with \(P\).  Thus
\[
        w_1qw_1^*+w_2qw_2^*\le p .
\]
Likewise \(a\in Q\ominus B\) and left multiplication by \(a\) sends every
first-letter \(P\) reduced word into a first-letter \(Q\) word, so
\[
        a p a^*\le q .
\]
Since \(S_{X_B}(N)\) is an \(N\)-bimodule and \(\varphi\) is \(N\)-central,
these inequalities give \(2\varphi(q)\le\varphi(p)\le\varphi(q)\), hence
\(\varphi(p)=\varphi(q)=0\).

The unitary \(h=w_1a\) is \(B\)-Haar: every non-zero power is an alternating
reduced word in centered \(P\)- and \(Q\)-letters, so \(E_B(h^n)=0\) for
\(n\ne0\).  For \(m\ne n\),
\[
h^ne_Bh^{-n}h^me_Bh^{-m}
 =h^n e_B h^{m-n}e_Bh^{-m}=h^nE_B(h^{m-n})e_Bh^{-m}=0 .
\]
The projections \(h^ne_Bh^{-n}\) are pairwise orthogonal and, by centrality,
have the same \(\varphi\)-value; hence \(\varphi(e_B)=0\).  This contradicts
\(1=\varphi(e_B+p+q)\).  By DKEP Theorem 6.2 this is precisely proper
proximality relative to \(X_B\) (and, in the factor case used below, agrees
with the normal-bidual criterion from Lemma 8.5).
\end{proof}

\section*{Application to graph products}

Fix \(v\in V\) and put \(L_v=\Lk_\Gamma(v)\).  The graph-product reduced-word
model, or \cite{CF17}, gives the standard amalgamated free product
decomposition
\[
        M\cong M_{V\setminus\{v\}}*_{M_{L_v}}
        (M_{L_v}\bbarotimes M_v).                                \tag{8}
\]
Let \(C(v)=\{r\ne v:r\not\sim_\Gamma v\}\).  Since \(\Gamma^c\) is connected,
\(C(v)\ne\emptyset\).  If \(C(v)\) contains distinct \(r,t\), choose trace-zero
unitaries \(u_r,u_t\) and set \(w_1=u_r,w_2=u_t\).  Then \(w_i\notin M_{L_v}\),
and the reduced-word expectation onto \(M_{L_v}\) kills \(w_i\) and
\(w_1^*w_2\).  If \(C(v)=\{r\}\), connectedness of \(\Gamma^c\) and
\(|V|\ge3\) give \(s\in L_v\) with \(s\not\sim_\Gamma r\); otherwise
\(\{v,r\}\) would be a component of \(\Gamma^c\).  Set
\(w_1=u_r,w_2=u_su_r\).  Here \(E_{M_{L_v}}(w_1)=0\),
\(E_{M_{L_v}}(w_2)=u_sE_{M_{L_v}}(u_r)=0\), and
\(w_1^*w_2=u_r^*u_su_r\) is a reduced word containing the outside vertex \(r\),
so its expectation onto \(M_{L_v}\) is \(0\).  Thus in all cases
\[
        E_{M_{L_v}}(w_i)=0,\qquad E_{M_{L_v}}(w_1^*w_2)=0 .
\]
A trace-zero unitary in \(M_v\) supplies the unitary \(a\) in (8), so
Proposition \ref{prop:BS} shows that \(M\) is properly proximal relative to
\(X_{M_{L_v}}\) for every \(v\).

Enumerate \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\).  Since no vertex belongs to its own link,
\(\cap_i L_{v_i}=\emptyset\).  Lemma \ref{lem:intersection} puts the associated
palindromic product in \(q_\emptyset\cA_Mq_\emptyset\).  Here
\(M_\emptyset=\C\), \(e_\C\) is the rank-one projection onto
\(\C\widehat1\), and DKEP Example 3.4 gives
\(X_{M_\emptyset}=\mathbb K(L^2M)\).

Finally, CDHJKN Theorem 2.4 implies that a join-irreducible graph product with
\(|V|\ge3\) and trace-zero vertex unitaries is a diffuse full factor.  A
diffuse amenable finite factor is the hyperfinite II\(_1\) factor and is not
full, so \(M\) is non-amenable.  It is separable because the graph is finite
and the vertices are separable.  Lemma \ref{lem:finite}, applied to the finite
family \(\{X_{M_{L_v}}:v\in V\}\), proves that \(M\) is properly proximal.
